title:
Inside an ABA
assessment.
caption: An ABA assessment and an autism diagnostic evaluation serve different purposes. An ABA assessment informs a proposed behavior-analytic care plan. This example shows four parts to discuss before attending: your perspective, observation, the findings and the proposed next step. The clinician determines the actual assessment.
slides: First, your perspective.
Discuss interests, communication, routines, existing support and the questions you want answered.
Then, observation.
The clinician chooses appropriate observations and activities. Ask what they are looking for and how comfort and breaks are handled.
Make sense of the findings.
Ask what was learned, what remains uncertain and how that informs the recommendation.
Discuss the proposed plan.
Ask why these goals, what the weekly commitment involves, what alternatives exist and how the plan will be reviewed.

title:
Before you arrive:
the small details.
caption: Knowing the entrance is useful. Knowing who will greet you, where you will wait and how to request a pause is useful too. These are practical details to confirm before a visit. The images show Kitewell’s fictional space concept; access arrangements must be confirmed with the actual clinic.
cta: Explore the spaces and arrival questions
slides: Find the entrance.
Confirm parking, the correct door and how to check in. Ask about mobility or access arrangements that matter to your family.
Make the arrival familiar.
Request a photo or simple visit sequence. Confirm who will welcome you and whether there may be a wait.
Discuss comfort beforehand.
Ask about noise, lighting, communication supports and breaks. Confirm any comfort items you would like to bring.

title:
What might
our family pay?
caption: An insurer’s name on a website is not an individual coverage decision. Before agreeing to care, request an explanation tied to the exact service, provider, location and plan. Ask about cost sharing, approval limits and charges outside covered care. Keep the estimate and the date of the review.
slides: Check the exact combination.
Which plan, provider, location and service were reviewed? Ask whether the provider is in network for that combination.
Understand your share.
What deductible remains? Does a copay or coinsurance apply? Ask how the proposed schedule affects the estimate.
Ask about limits and fees.
Confirm authorization dates or limits, excluded services, cancellation charges and what changes could require a new review.
Know who explains the bill.
Keep the estimate and contact name. Ask how to question a difference between the estimate, insurer statement and bill.

title:
Who is with
my child?
caption: The person providing a session may have a different role from the clinician responsible for the plan. A BCBA can assess, plan and supervise behavior-analytic services. An RBT works under supervision rather than independently. Ask for actual names, credentials, supervision arrangements and a contact for concerns.
cta: Understand the roles and supervision questions
slides: Who owns the care plan?
Ask who leads the assessment, explains recommendations, reviews progress and responds to clinical concerns.
Who provides direct support?
Ask who will work with your child, how that person is trained and supervised, and how staff changes are introduced.
When do we talk?
Confirm how caregiver updates work, how to reach the supervising clinician and what happens if you raise a concern.

title:
What if my child
doesn’t want to?
caption: A child’s communication can include words, gestures, actions or a communication device. Ask the provider how those signals shape participation, breaks and changes to a session. A parent should be able to question a method, discuss alternatives and understand the consent process. These are proposed care standards for the Kitewell concept.
cta: Read about comfort, choice and concerns
slides: Start with how they communicate.
Explain how your child shows interest, discomfort or a wish to stop. Ask how the team will learn and respond to those signals.
Ask what happens in the moment.
If your child does not want to participate, how does the team pause, adjust or reassess the activity? Ask for a concrete explanation.
Question the goal and method.
What is it intended to help with in daily life? What alternatives are available, and how are benefits and risks explained?
Know the route for concerns.
Confirm whom to contact, how a concern is reviewed and how to request changes or discuss ending a procedure or service.

title:
Can care fit
around school?
caption: A suitable plan has to be discussed alongside school, travel, work, other supports and family life. Ask for the proposed session frequency and duration, caregiver participation and review arrangements. An available afternoon slot does not determine clinically appropriate treatment hours.
slides: Write out the whole week.
Include school, travel, work, other supports and time to rest. Bring the practical constraints into the planning conversation.
Ask what care would involve.
Discuss proposed session length and frequency, caregiver meetings and any activities suggested outside sessions.
Ask about the unexpected.
How are illness, cancellations, staff changes and missed sessions handled? Confirm the contact and policy before agreeing.
Review the fit.
If the schedule is difficult to sustain, discuss that with the clinician. Availability and clinical recommendations are separate questions.

title:
On a waitlist?
Get a clear picture.
caption: A place on a waitlist is not a start date. Ask what affects a suitable opening, how the next update is agreed and how to change your preferences. If an estimate is offered, ask what it is based on and when it was last checked. Discuss other appropriate options with your child’s clinician while you wait.
slides: Understand the opening.
Is the wait for an assessment, an ongoing care place or both? Ask what must line up before an offer can be made.
Agree the next update.
Who will contact you, by which route, and when? A useful update should say what changed and what is still pending.
Keep preferences current.
Ask how to update location or scheduling preferences, and whether another appropriate option can be discussed.
Recheck before a start.
Coverage, required documents and clinical circumstances can change while waiting. Confirm what needs review before scheduling.

title:
Referral sent.
What comes back?
caption: A referral needs an acknowledgement that distinguishes receipt from readiness. The proposed Kitewell handoff identifies an intake owner, any outstanding items and the next action. Clinical suitability, plan requirements and availability are reviewed separately. Share records only through a verified clinic channel with the appropriate authority.
slides: Receipt is the first status.
Confirm that the referral reached the correct service and location. A receipt is not an assessment booking.
Make the next action specific.
Name the responsible contact, what is outstanding and who will obtain it. Avoid a generic “in progress” message.
Close the loop appropriately.
Agree how permitted status updates will reach the family and referring office, including when more information or another route is needed.

title:
A diagnosis.
An ABA assessment.
Different purposes.
caption: An inquiry opens a conversation about the service. A diagnostic evaluation considers developmental or diagnostic questions. An ABA assessment informs a proposed behavior-analytic plan. Kitewell’s concept does not offer diagnostic evaluations. If you are exploring developmental concerns, speak with your child’s pediatric clinician about an appropriate evaluation route.
cta: Find the starting point that matches your situation
slides: An inquiry
A conversation about scope, requirements and practical options. It does not confirm eligibility, coverage or an appointment.
A diagnostic evaluation
An evaluation of developmental or diagnostic questions by an appropriately qualified professional. This is outside Kitewell’s concept scope.
An ABA assessment
An individualized assessment to inform a proposed ABA plan. Ask what documents or referrals are required for the service and health plan.
